written: Written 21 Nov 2026. Figures in the tables update automatically; these summaries are refreshed separately.
themes: Share markets slump, led by AI and tech

US shares had their worst week since April 2025. The S&P 500 fell about 8.6% and is now in a “correction” (more than 10% below its peak); the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell about 10% and is now down for the year. Nvidia dropped 14% on Friday after a report that US regulators are examining its accounting, and Taiwan’s market had a record weekly fall. Safe havens such as the yen and US bonds gained.
A December Fed rise is now almost fully expected

Minutes of the Fed’s October meeting showed nearly all officials expect to raise rates in December, and two raised the idea of a bigger half-point move. New York Fed President Williams said there is no need for “dramatic action”. Futures on Friday put a quarter-point rise on 9 Dec at about 94%.
The dollar holds at a 19-month high

The dollar index was near 103.8, its fourth weekly gain. The euro fell below $1.10 for the first time since April 2025 and the pound slipped to about $1.31. The Australian dollar hit its lowest of 2026 (about 66.5 US cents) and the New Zealand dollar its lowest since 2020 (about 55 cents).
US bond yields ease but real yields stay high

The US 10-year yield ended the week near 4.92%, down from about 5.1%, as investors moved out of shares into bonds. After allowing for expected inflation, the 10-year “real” yield is still close to 2.9%; a government auction on 19 Nov sold at 2.90%, the highest in 24 years.
Gold and silver have their worst week since March

Gold fell about 8.7% to near $3,540 and silver to about $41, both the lowest in over a year. High real yields and a strong dollar hurt metals that pay no interest, and some investors sold them to cover losses on shares.
Oil falls for a third week

Brent ended at $92.57 (−3.4%) and WTI at $83.98 (−5.2%). Gulf exports are recovering, US crude stocks rose unexpectedly and the IEA now sees supply running ahead of demand. Attacks on ships near Hormuz continue. OPEC+ meets on 29 Nov to set 2027 output.

USD.note: Held at 3.75–4.00% on 28 Oct; two members (Cook and Hammack) wanted a rise. Minutes published on 18 Nov showed nearly all officials expect a rise in December, and two floated a half-point move; futures put a quarter-point rise on 9 Dec at about 94%.

EUR.note: Held on 29 Oct (deposit rate 2.50%) after two rises this year. Policymakers have said another rise is likely if the data hold, and markets now put a rise on 17 Dec at about 91%, up from about 72% a week earlier.

GBP.note: Raised to 4.00% on 5 Nov, its first rise since 2023, with all nine members voting to raise (Catherine Mann for 4.25%). Governor Bailey said on 18 Nov that the longer the Middle East conflict keeps energy prices high, the higher rates will need to be; markets put a rise on 17 Dec at about 80%.

JPY.note: Held at 1.25% on 30 Oct in an 8–1 vote (one member wanted a rise). Governor Ueda told parliament this week the bank should keep raising rates, and board member Takata called for moving quickly; markets put a rise to 1.50% at the 17–18 Dec meeting at roughly 75–85%.

CAD.note: Raised to 2.50% on 28 Oct, its first rise since July 2023, as oil pushes inflation up. Deputy Governor Gravelle said on 18 Nov that the high-oil risk has largely come true but gave no hint on December; estimates of the chance of another rise on 9 Dec range from about 40% to 65%.

AUD.note: Raised to 4.85% on 3 Nov in a 6–3 vote (three wanted to hold), its fifth rise this year. The minutes showed the three worried about rising unemployment and a sharper downturn; after weak jobs data, markets now expect a hold on 8 Dec and see the next move as a cut.

NZD.note: Surprised markets by holding at 2.75% on 28 Oct in a 4–3 vote (three wanted a rise). Governor Breman said on 19 Nov that fuel costs may be spreading into other prices; markets put a rise on 9 Dec at about 90%.

CHF.note: Held at 0% on 24 Sep and stands ready to sell francs if needed. Chairman Schlegel has said the bank “won’t hesitate” to act if inflation (1.5% in October) threatens price stability, but sees no broad spread of price pressure; the next decision is 10 Dec.

CNY.note: Lending rates unchanged again on 20 Nov (1-year 3.00%, 5-year 3.50%), the 18th month in a row; growth support comes mostly from the government. Factory-gate prices are rising fast (5.7%), so a rate cut looks unlikely; the next rate fixing is in December.

stories.USD: The Fed is set to raise rates again. Minutes of its October meeting showed nearly all officials expect a December rise, and some want to move faster. Data was mixed. Retail sales rose 0.2% in October (0.1% expected), and 0.6% without cars and petrol. The Philadelphia Fed factory survey fell to 6.3 from 20.9, while its prices-paid index jumped to 58.2. Jobless claims rose to 203,000. Consumer mood improved a little (51.5), and households now expect 3.7% inflation over the next year, down from 4.3%. Shares fell sharply, and the 10-year yield eased to about 4.92%. Next: business surveys (PMIs) 23 Nov, consumer confidence 24 Nov, Q3 GDP, core PCE inflation and jobless claims 25 Nov (UK 13:30), Thanksgiving holiday 26 Nov, November jobs report 4 Dec, Fed decision 9 Dec.
stories.EUR: Inflation is high. Final figures confirmed 4.0% in October, the highest in three years, mainly because of energy; core inflation (without food and energy) was revised up to 2.6%. Markets now put the chance of an ECB rise on 17 Dec at about 91%. Investor mood improved: the ZEW survey rose to 26.5 (19.1 expected) and to 35.6 in Germany. Consumer confidence edged up to −16.9. The ECB’s twice-yearly financial stability review warned that high AI share prices, increasingly funded by debt, and heavy government borrowing are key risks. The euro fell below $1.10 for the first time since April 2025, as US rates look set to rise faster. Next: business surveys (PMIs) 23 Nov (UK 08:15–09:00), final consumer confidence 27 Nov, November inflation 1 Dec, ECB decision 17 Dec.
stories.GBP: UK inflation rose to 3.6% in October, a one-year high and in line with forecasts. Petrol prices, up 33% on a year, gave the biggest push; core inflation stayed at 2.8% and services inflation at 3.7%. The jobs market is cooling: payrolls fell 34,000 in October, vacancies dropped to 690,000 and regular pay growth slowed to 3.5%, though unemployment fell to 4.6%. Shoppers bounced back, with retail sales up 0.7% in October against no change expected. Governor Bailey said rates may need to go higher if energy stays dear; markets put a 17 Dec rise at about 80%. The pound slipped to about $1.31. Next: business surveys (PMIs) 23 Nov (UK 09:30), Bank officials before MPs 25 Nov, Financial Stability Report 26 Nov, rate decision 17 Dec.
stories.JPY: Japan’s economy stalled in Q3. Output was flat on the quarter (−0.1% at an annual rate) as household spending fell 0.3% and exports slipped, while business investment rose 1.6%. Inflation picked up to 2.3% in October; core inflation (without fresh food) was 2.2%, a little below the 2.3% expected. Even so, the Bank of Japan sounds ready to raise rates: Governor Ueda told parliament the bank should keep raising because conditions are still loose, and most economists expect a rise to 1.50% in December. The dollar peaked just under ¥160 on 19 Nov, then the yen strengthened to about ¥158.8 as share markets fell. The finance minister repeated warnings against rapid moves. Next: market holiday 23 Nov, Tokyo inflation 26 Nov (UK 23:30), BoJ decision 18 Dec.
stories.CAD: Inflation held at 3.1% in October, a little below the 3.2% expected. Petrol was up 30.9% on a year, but without food and energy prices rose only 1.8%, and rent growth slowed. Shoppers spent 0.8% more in September, mostly at petrol stations, but an early estimate points to a 1.5% fall in October. Governor Macklem said he will not seek a second term and will leave in June 2027. The jobs market is weak (unemployment 6.7%), and views on a December rate rise are split. The Canadian dollar fell to around C$1.43 per US dollar, its weakest since April 2025, as US rates look set to rise faster and oil fell. Next: Macklem speaks 24 Nov, Q3 GDP 30 Nov, November jobs 4 Dec, rate decision 9 Dec.
stories.AUD: Australia’s jobs market weakened sharply. Employment fell by 43,500 in October, after a 39,300 fall in September, and unemployment jumped to 4.9%, the highest since 2021. Wages rose 1.1% in the quarter (3.5% on a year), a little faster than expected. Minutes of the RBA’s November meeting showed three of nine members wanted to hold, citing rising unemployment, falling house prices and the risk of a sharper downturn. Markets now expect the RBA to hold on 8 Dec and have started to price rate cuts by late 2027. Inflation was 4.3% in September, well above the 2–3% target. The Australian dollar fell to about 66.5 US cents, its lowest this year. Next: October inflation 25 Nov (UK 00:30), Bullock speaks 1 Dec, Q3 GDP 2 Dec, RBA decision 8 Dec.
stories.NZD: New Zealand’s central bank looks set to raise rates. Businesses now expect inflation of 2.92% over the next year, up from 2.60%, and Governor Breman warned on 19 Nov that fuel costs may be feeding into other prices. Markets put a rise on 9 Dec at about 90%. The economy is weak, though: unemployment is 5.7% and jobs fell in the September quarter. October’s trade deficit was NZ$2.8bn, much wider than expected, as imports of fuel and aircraft rose. Inflation is 3.7% (Q3). Coalition talks after the 7 Nov election are in their last stages. The kiwi fell to about 55 US cents, its lowest since 2020. Next: Q3 retail sales 22 Nov (UK 21:45), final election result 27 Nov, RBNZ decision 9 Dec.
stories.CHF: Swiss inflation rose to 1.5% in October, the highest since late 2023, mostly because of fuel and heating oil; core inflation stayed low at 0.5%. An early estimate shows the economy grew 0.2% in Q3, and exports rose in October. The SNB keeps its rate at 0% and says it is ready to sell francs if the currency gets too strong, while Chairman Schlegel sees no broad spread of price pressure. Markets expect no change in December. The franc weakened against the dollar this week: the dollar reached about 0.844 francs on 19 Nov, an 18-month high, as US rates look set to rise. The franc is a safe haven, so it can gain when global worries rise. Next: full Q3 GDP 30 Nov, November inflation 2 Dec, SNB decision 10 Dec.
stories.CNY: China is shown because it drives AUD, NZD and commodity demand. October data was weak. Retail sales grew just 0.4% on a year (0.8% expected) and factory output 4.8% (5.3% expected). Investment in factories, roads and buildings is down 8.1% so far this year, and property investment is down 21.6%. New home prices fell 2.4% on a year, though that is the smallest drop in almost a year. Unemployment eased to 5.1%. Lending rates were left unchanged for an 18th month (1-year 3.00%), and no new stimulus was announced. Consumer inflation is only 0.7%, but factory-gate prices are up 5.7%. The yuan is strong, near 6.67 per dollar, around its strongest since 2022. Next: industrial profits next week, official business surveys (PMIs) at the end of November.

oil.title: Oil (WTI and Brent)
oil.what: The price of crude oil. Brent is the global benchmark, WTI the US one.
oil.now: Brent ended the week at $92.57 and WTI at $83.98, a third weekly fall (−3.4% and −5.2%). That is about 11% below late May (Brent about $104), and WTI touched its lowest since August this week. Gulf exports are recovering, US crude stocks rose unexpectedly, and the IEA says supply is now running ahead of demand, with stocks building. Shipping costs from the Gulf have dropped sharply, a sign traders see less danger. The risk has not gone: tankers near Oman were attacked on 16 Nov, Houthi drones targeted Saudi pipeline sites, and Iran wants the US blockade lifted before it reopens Hormuz. OPEC+ meets on 29 Nov to set 2027 output.
oil.links: High oil helps oil exporters (CAD) and hurts importers (JPY, EUR). It feeds straight into inflation, which is why central banks have turned to raising rates. Falling oil has added to the Canadian dollar’s weakness.

gold.title: Gold
gold.what: Gold priced in US dollars. It pays no interest, so it competes with what investors can earn elsewhere.
gold.now: Around $3,540, down about 8.7% this week, its worst week since March and its lowest since September 2025. That is about 21% lower than in late May (about $4,500) and roughly 37% below January’s record near $5,595. Markets see a December Fed rise as almost certain, the 10-year real yield is near 2.9% and the dollar is at a 19-month high. During the share sell-off some investors sold gold to cover losses. Central banks are still buying: they added a net 321 tonnes in Q3, according to the World Gold Council.
gold.links: Gold tends to rise when real yields fall, the dollar weakens or fear spikes. It often moves with CHF and JPY as a safe haven, and with AUD, since Australia is a big producer.

silver.title: Silver
silver.what: Half precious metal, half industrial metal (solar panels, electronics), so it swings more than gold.
silver.now: Around $41, its lowest in over a year, down roughly 15% this week. It is roughly 46% lower than in late May (about $76) and about two-thirds below January’s peak near $120. It faces the same rate headwind as gold, plus worries about factory demand as tech and AI shares slump.
silver.links: Follows gold in direction but with bigger swings; weaker Chinese industry weighs on it.
